title: How the Care Leaver Apprenticeship Bursary supported my journey, by Grace

content.content: My name is Grace, and I am currently completing a Customer Service Practitioner Level 2 apprenticeship with Ginger Nut Training after progressing from a scholarship.

Before this, I didn’t even understand how a modern-day apprenticeship worked, let alone how much one could change my life. I’m now working as a Client Engagement Administrator, supporting employers and learners throughout their apprenticeship journey. At 20 years old, I’ve found a real sense of purpose in helping others access opportunities that can change their lives, just as mine was changed. Every day, I’m building new skills, growing in confidence, and proving to myself that my past doesn’t have to define my future.

Like many care leavers, I faced challenges that many young people don’t have to think about. Starting an apprenticeship is exciting, but it can also be financially difficult, especially when you’re transitioning into independence. Although I am earning a living wage, I still have to pay my own way. Including rent, bills, saving and making arrangements to spend quality time with my siblings.
How the Care Leaver Apprenticeship Bursary helped me

I first found out about the Care Leaver Apprenticeship Bursary through my job role, working for a training provider and training under them. The process of accessing it was well explained and very straightforward for me, I felt supported throughout. Knowing that this funding was available made me feel that care leavers were being recognised and given support to succeed, rather than being expected to overcome every challenge on our own.
I decided to use my payments of the bursary towards buying my first car, and I can honestly say it has been one of the best decisions I have ever made.

Having a car has completely changed my experience. The impact has gone far beyond simply having transport. Owning a car has given me confidence and independence. It has allowed me to become more self-sufficient and has opened up opportunities that may not have been possible otherwise.

For me, the bursary wasn’t just financial support. It was an investment in my future. It removed one of the barriers that could have made completing my apprenticeship much more difficult and helped me build a stronger foundation for my career.

The opportunities I've had have been incredible. I've spoken in Parliament about improving apprenticeship opportunities for care leavers, been invited to speak on panels and at national events to share my experiences and been recognised as a finalist for Apprentice of the Year. I was also proud to become an ambassador in a role that promotes helping youth into work.

It's amazing to see how far I've come. My apprenticeship has given me much more than qualifications, it has given me confidence, purpose and the belief that I can achieve things I once thought were out of reach. I'm now excited to continue my journey by progressing onto a higher-level apprenticeship, building on everything I've learned so far and continuing to develop both personally and professionally.
My advice to other care leavers, employers and training providers

My advice to other care leavers is simple - don't be afraid to ask about the support that is available. I know it can sometimes feel like you're expected to manage everything on your own, but the Care Leaver Apprenticeship Bursary exists because people recognise that care leavers may face additional challenges.

Taking advantage of that support isn't a weakness, it's giving yourself the best possible chance to succeed. I also think it should be said that it doesn’t have to be used in the same way as I did, while having a car is a huge achievement for me, having a pot of money to support any finances and take away worries is just as huge of an achievement.

I would also encourage employers and training providers to actively promote the bursary. There may be care leavers who don't realise they are entitled to it, and something as simple as telling them about the funding could make a life changing difference. Whether it helps someone pay for travel, buy equipment, or gain greater independence like it did for me, the impact can last long after the apprenticeship has finished.
Unfortunately, the bursary remains underclaimed, meaning too many eligible care leavers are missing out on support that could make a real difference to their lives.

If you're a care leaver thinking about an apprenticeship, ask your training provider about the Care Leaver Apprenticeship Bursary and what support is available. It could be the helping hand that makes all the difference, just as it did for me.  Employers and training providers, make sure your apprentices know about the bursary. Training providers claim on behalf of apprentices.
See guidance here: Apprenticeships care leavers’ bursary guidance - GOV.UK

title: Managing farms and land during prolonged dry weather and drought

content.content: Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought after experiencing record-low rainfall and unusually high temperatures.
So far in August, rainfall has been 5% of the seasonal average, following the driest July in 190 years.

This summer has been hard for farmers. Dry conditions are placing pressure on farm businesses. Grass growth has reduced, forage is less available, crops are being affected and water supplies are under pressure. Farmers are also facing higher fertiliser and red diesel costs because of the conflict in the Middle East.
Food security is national security, which is why we are working closely with farmers, the Environment Agency and the water sector during this exceptionally dry weather.

Defra met with farming and food representatives on Wednesday 5 August to discuss solutions to the challenges the dry weather presents. The National Drought Group met on Monday 10 August and will continue to co-ordinate the broader impacts of dry weather.

We are looking at how we can support farmers through this prolonged dry weather and hope to be able to say more on this soon, alongside how we're building greater long-term resilience to climate shocks.
In this blog post, we've gathered information and resources to help farmers and growers understand what support is available and what steps you can take now.
Access to water
Environment Agency guidance on abstraction and irrigation
If prolonged dry weather is affecting your access to water, there may be options available to help you.
Colleagues at the Environment Agency have published a dedicated blog bringing together drought advice, abstraction updates and useful resources for farmers and growers on the following:
The Environment Agency can advise farmers on measures available during drought. These include options that sit outside usual abstraction licence conditions.
If you have any questions, you can call their National Customer Contact Centre for advice on 03708 506 506.
Managing reservoirs
Extreme weather can impact the safety of your reservoir.
During periods of drought, regularly check reservoir levels and inspect embankments, spillways and surrounding areas for signs of cracking or damage caused by dry ground conditions.
It’s also important to manage vegetation and reduce fire risks around reservoirs and infrastructure.
Further advice is available on GOV.UK on how to manage, maintain and improve your reservoir in extreme weather.
Storage of flammable materials
High temperatures and prolonged dry weather can increase the fire risk for hay, straw and other materials.

Where possible, move hay and straw into storage promptly after harvest, ensuring that moisture levels are sufficiently low. Damp hay can generate heat as it dries, creating a risk of spontaneous combustion.
Sections 2 and 4 of the NFU's Risk Management Programme for the Prevention of Fires on Farms sets this out in further detail.

Where possible, keep hay and straw storage away from other farm buildings, particularly those which house fuel, fertiliser, chemicals or other combustible materials. Try to leave adequate space between stacks where possible.
Devon and Somerset's Fire and Rescue Service have created this page on monitoring hay and straw temperatures.
Animal health & welfare
Hot, dry weather can place additional pressure on the health and wellbeing of livestock and increase demand for water.
Make sure animals have sufficient drinking water, check them regularly for signs of heat stress, and have their management or diets adjusted if necessary.
It’s also worth planning ahead for potential water shortages, identifying alternative water sources, and where required, planning arrangements to move animals.
Visit GOV.UK for more advice on caring for farm animals and horses in extreme weather.
Wildfire & creating firebreaks
Mitigating fire risks

Many parts of the country are at a very high or exceptional risk of fire. You can check to see the fire risk in your area in these Fire Severity Index (FSI) maps, provided by the Met Office, for the whole of England and Wales.

This Farmland Safety and Fire Prevention booklet produced by the Fire & Rescue services, in partnership with the NFU, examines the fire dangers which are commonly found on farms. It identifies simple ways in which risks can be reduced.
Creating firebreaks
In areas facing a high risk of wildfire, creating firebreaks can help limit the spread of fire and protect livestock, farm equipment, homes, and crops where they have not already been harvested.

Firebreaks are created by removing or managing flammable vegetation, such as long, dry grass. This can include cutting, clearing or ploughing. Reducing vegetation limits the fuel available to a fire and helps contain it. It also exposes bare soil that flames cannot easily cross.

To be effective, the width of the firebreak should be around 3 times the height of the highest crop or vegetation next to it. For example, if your wheat crop is around 1 metre high, the firebreak would be around 3 metres wide as a minimum.
If you’re considering creating a firebreak, make sure you comply with all relevant law and regulatory requirements which apply to you and your land.

If your land is in an Environmental Land Management (ELM) revenue agreement, you must contact the RPA before you create a firebreak on that land. Read the ‘ELM revenue schemes’ information below to find out how to do this.
Controlled burning of heather, grassland and crop residue
In areas that are suffering from extended periods of dry weather, undertaking routine controlled burning significantly increases the likelihood of a wildfire starting.

For the safety of your local community, Defra is advising farmers to not burn heather, rough grass or other vegetation, even if you have a licence, consent or agreement that permits you to burn at this time of year.
Farmers and land owners should continue to work with the Fire & Rescue Service who, in the event of a live incident, may undertake tactical burns to create a fuel break.
Schemes and grants
ELM revenue schemes
We recognise that prolonged hot and dry weather can create challenges for farmers and land managers delivering actions under our ELM revenue schemes.
We are actively considering whether we need to make temporary adjustments to ELM revenue agreements under the following schemes:
We will provide a further update on any temporary adjustments as soon as possible.
In the meantime, if extreme weather prevents you from meeting your ELM agreement requirements, you must tell the RPA:
The RPA will use the information you provide to decide what action to take. If there is any impact on your payments they will tell you the outcome of any decisions in writing.
Innovation & technology
Through the Farming Innovation Programme, we’re supporting farmers to implement innovative technologies that help use water more efficiently.

Trying something new can involve time, cost and uncertainty. Grants like the Accelerating Development of Practices and Technologies (ADOPT) fund helps reduce that risk by funding practical, on-farm trials and demonstrations led by farmers.
This includes projects trialling new technologies for conserving water on farm, such as this smart irrigation trial led by Water Resources East.
ADOPT has a rolling application window, you can find out how to apply by visiting the Innovate UK website.
Local Resource Option Screening Studies

We launched the latest round of Local Resource Option (LRO) Screening Studies earlier this summer. These studies support groups of farmers to identify practical solutions to improve long-term water resilience.
The application window for 2026/27 is now closed and projects selected.

However, if you would like to be considered on a first-come-first-served basis (subject to eligibility criteria), we may be able to offer further projects. This could happen if funds remain after the currently selected projects are awarded to contractors.
Please contact WRAgriculture@environment-agency.gov.uk for more information.
Further Information
Subscribe to the Defra Farming Blog to be the first to find out further information on guidance and support for managing your farm through periods of drought.
By subscribing, you’ll receive an email whenever a new post is published.

description: Almost three-quarters of land in England is now in drought after experiencing record-low rainfall and unusually high temperatures. As the dry weather looks set to persist, we've gathered information and resources to help farmers and growers.

title: How does the Environment Agency manage abstraction to protect the environment?

content.content: Water is essential for drinking, farming, industry, wildlife and recreation. Managing our rivers, lakes, estuaries, wetlands and groundwater properly ensures the needs of society, the economy and nature can be met over the long term.
2026 has seen the driest July in 190 years, with just 5 per cent of expected rainfall.

This has placed significant demands on abstraction, particularly for irrigation, and agricultural reservoir stocks have declined rapidly, especially where abstractors rely heavily on storage. If you own, operate or are planning to build a reservoir, our new planning guides explain the requirements.

Sustainable water abstraction is essential to ensure that river flows and groundwater levels support ecology and natural resilience. We work with abstractors to balance the needs of the public, industry, farmers and the environment.
What are abstraction licences?

Abstraction is the process of taking water from a river, lake or groundwater source for uses such as irrigation, industry, recreation or drinking water. The Environment Agency grants abstraction licences to protect the environment and the rights of existing lawful water users.
Those with abstraction licences are allowed to take water in line with the conditions of their licence.

Abstracting more than 20 cubic metres a day generally requires a licence, though some activities, such as firefighting, are exempt. If you take water from the same source at multiple points, the combined total must be 20 cubic metres or less a day to qualify for exemption.

If you don't hold a licence, you may be able to agree a trade or share with an existing licence holder, permanently or temporarily, provided all licence conditions can still be met. Where an abstraction is moved to a different abstraction point, the buyer of the abstraction right would normally have to apply for their own licence or change their existing licence if they have one.
Not all activities require an abstraction licence to take place with some being exempt.
Abstraction licence holders can manage their accounts online to see a summary of their licence and past returns.
How can the Environment Agency restrict abstraction?
There are two main types of restrictions that the Environment Agency can implement on abstractors at times of pressure: hands-off flow conditions and Section 57 restrictions.

Hands-off flow conditions on licences reduce or prevent abstraction to protect other abstractors and the environment. Many of these restrictions have come into effect in 2026 due to very low river flows. Licence holders who have hands-off flow condition on their licences will be notified when the condition comes into force, with as much advance notice as possible.
Section 57 of the Water Resources Act 1991 allows formal notices to be issued to holders of spray irrigation abstraction licences to protect river flows during drought throughout a catchment.
Spray irrigation abstraction licence holders can help make the most of the water which their licence authorises to take by:
Environment Agency updated prospects for irrigation report for summer 2026 can be found on gov.uk.

We work closely with farmers, the National Farmers Union (NFU), Water Abstraction Groups (WAGs) and Internal Drainage Boards (IDBs) to give as much advanced notice as possible before cessation conditions are needed on abstraction licences to protect the environment.
We continue to carry out irrigation patrols and other compliance checks to ensure all abstractors are complying with their licence conditions to help protect water availability.

If abstractors believe that they may not be able to comply with their abstraction licence or have issues accessing water supplies, they should contact their local area office for further advice as soon as possible.
What support is available for those with abstraction licences who may have restrictions in place?
General guidance is available for abstraction licence holders affected by prolonged dry weather and drought, alongside short and long-term options to improve water access and resilience.
For short term support:
Managing abstraction for the long term
In the longer term, there are a number of schemes for abstractors that can help generate water resilience listed below.
Reporting incidents
If you are out and about, please report incidents to our hotline  - 0800 80 70 60.
It's free and open 24 hours a day.
Incidents you should report include:
More information on other incidents and how to report can be found on gov.uk.
For any further questions you can call our National Customer Contact Centre on 03708 506 506.

title: Can technology improve people’s experience of organisational change?

content.content: Change is a human challenge

In the Civil Service, organisational change is a reality. Teams evolve, priorities shift, and departments periodically go through restructures, machinery of government changes, and workforce redesign programmes. While each change programme is different, they all have one thing in common: they affect people.

Change is ultimately a human challenge. It impacts careers, wellbeing, and confidence in the organisation. Technology cannot solve those challenges, but it can support the processes around them by making them more transparent, consistent and fair.

I became involved in a large organisational restructure because the allocation process presented exactly that kind of opportunity. The restructure involved allocating a large number of people across multiple grades, limited vacancies and competing preferences, all within a complex set of agreed business rules. Managing this fairly and consistently through a manual process was increasingly difficult. The challenge was not simply to make the process faster, but to reduce risk and give people greater confidence in the outcome.
The experience reinforced an important lesson: when technology is used in people-focused decisions, transparency and accountability must come before sophistication.
The challenge of organisational restructure

The existing allocation process involved significant manual effort. Candidates could express preferences across multiple roles, vacancies were limited, and allocations needed to consider scores, preferences and redeployment rules simultaneously.
Managing this process manually created several challenges, including:
Most importantly, long processing times meant people spent longer waiting for clarity about their future roles.
The objective was therefore not simply operational efficiency. It was to reduce the risks associated with complex manual processing to improve outcomes for the people involved.
Using technology to support (not replace) decision making
At the heart of the solution was an allocation algorithm that matched candidates to roles.
The word "algorithm" can sometimes imply automated decision-making. In this case, the system acted more like a transparent administrative process than an AI model.
The algorithm was “deterministic”, which meant it followed a defined sequence of rules:

Importantly, the system did not learn, predict or optimise like an AI model. It simply applied the agreed rules consistently and at scale. Every allocation could be traced back to documented rules and independently verified.
Choosing automation over artificial intelligence was a deliberate choice to ensure:
Ethics and governance
Governance and ethical oversight were built into the project from the outset.
Alongside HR and trade union engagement, we worked with the departmental ethics committee to review the proposed approach.

The allocation process was never intended to replace human judgement. Cases that could not be resolved automatically were escalated for review. Decision-makers retained the ability to challenge or override outcomes where there was a clear and documented rationale.
This early engagement helped shape both the design and the governance framework, while keeping stakeholders informed of the benefits of the approach prior to implementation.
Testing and assurance
Before deployment, we ran the allocation process in parallel with the existing manual method.
This allowed us to:
The comparison demonstrated that the automated approach produced consistent and explainable outcomes while dramatically reducing processing time.
Impact
The system reduced a process that previously took days to complete to a matter of seconds. But its most important benefits were not technical.

For the people involved, this meant less time waiting for clarity during an uncertain period. For decision-makers, it created a transparent, auditable record of every allocation, reduced the working hours needed to complete the process, and made each decision easier to explain.

The manual method used for comparison produced several errors that the algorithm did not. There was only one instance where the human reviewer overrode the algorithm’s output: allocating someone their second choice freed up their first-choice role for an unallocated candidate.
The experience shows that government organisations do not always need advanced AI to solve complex problems.
What’s next?
There are clear lessons for organisational change across government.

Many workforce and organisational challenges involve large volumes of information, complex business rules and significant consequences for individuals. These are exactly the situations where well-designed automation can add value.

The approach is also highly replicable. Because the solution relies on documented business rules rather than specialist AI models, it can be adapted by other departments facing similar allocation or prioritisation challenges.
Successful change is about improving outcomes for people. This can be supported with technology by involving users and ethics committees from the beginning.
Conclusion

If there is one takeaway from this work, it is that technology should make important decisions easier to understand, not harder.  You do not always need AI to solve complex public-sector problems. Well-designed automation can support decision making while remaining understandable and auditable.

For organisations that feel cautious about using technology in sensitive decisions, the lesson is simple: start with explainability. People’s confidence in your solution will grow when they can understand how the system works, challenge its outputs and see that human judgement remains part of the process.
If you would like to know more about the algorithm or would like advice on replicating our work, please reach out in the comments.

description: What role can automation play in organisational change? Drawing on a government restructure, this blog shows how digital transformation helped deliver fairer, more transparent outcomes while reducing risk and manual effort.

title: Coverage of the government's High Streets announcement

content.content: There has been widespread national, regional and broadcast coverage of the government’s announcement on improving Britain’s high streets.

The Guardian, The Times, The Independent, The Daily Telegraph and The Financial Times, The i Paper, BBC News and Metro all ran pieces noting the new measures announced by the Prime Minister which are designed to give councils and local communities greater control over their high streets, including powers to block new vape shops, betting shops and adult gaming centres.
The announcement was also picked up by the The Daily Mail, The Daily Express and the Daily Star.

There is also extensive coverage across regional outlets including The MEN, The Standard, CityAM, The York Press, Birmingham Live, Eastern Daily Press, Liverpool Echo, Lancashire Telegraph, Cambridgeshire Live, Somerset Live, Bristol Live, Devon Live, The Northern Echo, Wales Online, Leeds Live, and The Star.
Communities Secretary Angela Rayner was interviewed by BBC Radio 4 Today, BBC Breakfast, LBC and GMB on the morning round.
There has been further coverage on broadcast including on BBC News, ITV News, GB News, Sky News, LBC News among others alongside regional outlets such as BBC Look North, BBC London and BBC Northwest.

Radio coverage includes BBC Radio 1, BBC Radio 1Xtra, BBC Radio 4, BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 6, LBC News, Sky News Radio, Heart Kent, Times Radio, talk Radio, Hits Radio East Midlands, and Greatest Hits who all covered the story in afternoon bulletins.
The announcement has also featured on Channel 5’s Jeremy Vine and Storm and Alex daytime programming.
Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner said:

"People know when their high street isn't working for them. Whether it’s the vape shop or betting shops that's opened with no say from locals, the shopfront that's seen better days, or the sense that nobody's in control.
“These problems have built up over years, but this government won't leave councils and communities powerless to crackdown on everyday eyesores that blight our high streets.
"That's why we're giving local leaders the power to say no to what doesn't belong on their high street, and the tools to fix it themselves.”

title: How we’re helping people and businesses get help from APHA with sustainable design

content.content: Senior content designer Eleanor Shakeshaft and senior service designer Ibarieze Abani from the APHA improving customer experience team discuss how they’re improving the way customers get support when they can't find the answers they need online.

In our team’s first blog post, we explained our choice of tools and technology. Here, we zoom in further to look at how workshopping with colleagues in customer service teams has been instrumental in shaping how we build a more sustainable service.
To recap, our team’s goals are to:
Simplifying the journey to get help
When customers need support from APHA, there are two steps in their journey:
Historically, these journeys could be difficult to navigate. Customers were often presented with long lists of email addresses and contact routes, leaving them to decide which team could help.

65% of APHA's customer emails were sent to the wrong team and needed to be redirected. This was a poor experience for customers who had to wait longer for a reply and was an inefficient use of time for CSC teams.
To address this, we've focused on both stages of the experience.
Helping customers find the right team
One of the main entry points for users needing support is the page previously known as Contact APHA.
This page is now titled Get help with animal and plant health. We renamed it because research showed this wording was more intuitive to users.
We're also testing a user-centred routing tool that helps people find the right team based on what they're trying to do.
It uses familiar language and does the hard work of getting customers to the right team, instead of expecting them to understand APHA's internal structure.
This makes it quicker and easier for customers to get the help they need.
Making it easier to get in touch
The biggest change to customers is replacing many of APHA's email addresses with contact forms.
Moving away from email to contact forms and a Contact Centre as a Service (CCaaS) platform has several benefits, including:
However, delivering this change at scale presented a challenge.
A large number of services and contact routes were in scope. We needed a way to design and roll out forms at pace, without creating entirely bespoke solutions for every team.
Learning from a pilot approach
We started with a pilot in Alpha, working closely with two service areas: pet travel and customer advice.
This allowed us to:
The pilot approach gave us valuable insight into how different teams worked. But it quickly became clear it wouldn't be an efficient way to deliver contact forms at scale.
The early forms were highly tailored to individual services. This required significant collaboration and refinement to accommodate complex policy needs.
We also discovered many CSC teams handle a broader range of work than expected, including specialist applications and processes.
Stepping back to see the bigger picture
To create a more scalable solution, we took a step back and looked across the wider CSC landscape.
Through workshops with teams, we explored:
This helped us move from designing individual forms to designing a reusable pattern.
We combined the insights from these workshops with a set of design principles and practical constraints. For example, limiting the number of fields in the first iteration of a form.
The end result was a contact form pattern that could be applied across multiple services,
Taking this approach has allowed us to co-design with teams and publish forms more efficiently and sustainable, without compromising on quality and consistency for customers.
A pattern in action: reporting a farm animal welfare concern
One example of this approach can be seen in the 'Report a farm animal welfare concern' service.

Although this service sits slightly outside the scope of the wider ‘getting help’ work, it is an important priority area for APHA. Given the scope and timelines, designing a service entirely from scratch wasn't practical.
Instead, we looked at other similar Defra services to identify patterns we could reuse.
Patterns gave us:
Rather than reinventing the wheel, we were able to build on existing good practice and focus our effort on aspects unique to the service.
Designing for the future
This work is about more than replacing inboxes with forms.

We’re adding patterns and components like this to the Defra Digital service manual to be reused by other teams. This will reduce the time and resources needed to design from scratch for similar services.
This approach supports Defra's ambitions to invest in reusable products and common platforms, rather than creating one-off solutions for individual programmes.
This will enable us to improve user experience, scale delivery, reduce duplication and improve consistency across Defra.
More information
Eleanor Shakeshaft is a Senior content designer and Ibarieze Abani  a senior service designer  with the APHA improving customer experience team .

If you're interested in finding out more about what we do in Defra Digital Data Technology and Security check out our LinkedIn page for all the latest news, stories and job openings. While you're there, why not give us a follow?
Like what you read? Subscribe to the blog for all the latest updates.

title: Championing Youth Talent in the Civil Service

content.content: Today, 12th August we celebrate International Youth Day and recognise the potential, resilience, and ambition of young people.

This year, the official theme is ‘Different Contexts, Common Aspirations’. It is a powerful reminder that while young people grow up facing different realities and structural barriers, their desires for dignity, security, and a meaningful career remain universal.
Here in the Civil Service, this theme strikes at the very heart of Going Forward into Employment (GFiE). We know that talent is everywhere, but opportunity is not.

To build a modern Civil Service that truly reflects the public it serves, we must actively open our doors to young people whose background or lack of experience might limit their opportunity for employment.
Beyond the Traditional CV
For many young people, standard recruitment processes can feel like a huge hurdle.

Consider a neurodivergent young person for whom a standard competency based interview tests social performance rather than actual capability. Or consider a young person trying to rebuild their life after time in the justice system, or one who has experienced long-term unemployment and lacks work experience.
Relying solely on polished CVs and standard recruitment processes sometimes risks filtering out brilliant, resilient talent.
Bridging the Gap

GFiE provides support through a dedicated network of pathways, and using Exceptions to the Civil Service Recruitment Principles, we provide work experience and fixed-term entry roles for Young People.

We look at potential, problem-solving, and strengths. Just as importantly, we ensure that once these young people join us, they receive wrap-around support from line managers,  buddies and workplace adjustments, enabling young people to thrive in their new careers.
A Mutual Aspiration

GFiE isn't just about the Civil Service helping young people; it is about the Civil Service needing them. Young people aspire to secure fulfilling roles, and we aspire to deliver the best possible public services.

When we bring in a young person who has navigated complex personal challenges, or who looks at problems through a neurodivergent lens, we aren't just filling a vacancy. We are injecting our departments with incredible adaptability, fresh perspectives, and a deep, lived understanding of the communities we serve. Their aspirations drive our innovation.

Bethany joined the DWP through a social mobility apprenticeship. Her experience may be different from that of many young people, but her aspirations were the same: to find stability, build a career and create a brighter future. Through a Social Mobility Apprenticeship with DWP, she was given the opportunity to do just that.
Pathways into the Civil Service for Young Talent

GFiE operates an expanding network of recruitment pathways, many of which are designed specifically to support young people - including those who are Not in Education, Employment, or Training (NEET), into fulfilling careers.

As we celebrate International Youth Day, we are asking hiring managers, team leaders, and senior civil servants across every department a simple question: Are you ready to open doors within your teams to provide opportunities for Young People
By providing a vacancy through a GFiE pathway, you aren't just changing a young person's life chances, you are giving an opportunity to eager young talent to show their potential.

title: The UK NSC’s prostate cancer screening model will remain open and under review

content.content: The UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC) makes recommendations to ministers in the 4 UK countries about all aspects of screening.

At its meeting in March 2026, the independent scientific committee recommended the introduction of the UK’s first prostate cancer screening programme, targeted at one cohort of men with specific gene variants. This recommendation was informed by an updated modelling study carried out by experts at the Sheffield Centre of Health and Related Research (SCHARR).

As announced in May, the government is commissioning and funding SCHARR to maintain this model for a further 3 years and continue its work with the UK NSC. This means significant new data and evidence can be considered for inclusion in the model throughout the life of the contract. Evidence will be considered for inclusion where it is of high quality, has been peer reviewed and is available in the public literature.

The SCHARR model uses data and evidence from a variety of sources. Some of this information – for example, epidemiological data and NHS costs – will need to be kept updated on a rolling basis throughout the 3-year period to ensure the most up-to-date and relevant data is used before any new analyses are run.
The SCHARR team and the UK NSC secretariat are already working to identify and consider new evidence, including:

If this new evidence is found to meet the criteria for inclusion specified above, then the model will be adjusted to allow for different risk-stratified screening pathways for men based on the results of multiple tests.

In addition, the UK NSC secretariat is liaising with the research team running the TRANSFORM trial, which is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR). The UK NSC will work with SCHARR to ensure the model is updated where any significant information emerges from this large-scale research trial, especially evidence relating to the screening of Black men.
Findings from the live model will be considered carefully and inform future UK NSC recommendations.

The UK NSC 2026 open call for topics is open until 30 September.  Any open call submissions related to new evidence on prostate cancer can also be considered for inclusion in the model, if appropriate.

title: What the government is doing to improve your high streets

content.content: A HELPING HAND FOR OUR HIGH STREETS
🗣️ Today, the government is giving local people and councils a real say over what opens on their high street.
🏚️ Too many high streets have been taken over by endless vape shops, gambling premises and other businesses that don't do much for the local community. That's about to change.
🛠️ New powers mean local people and councils can finally take back control of their shops, as part of the Prime Minister's plan to save Britain's high streets.
THE PROBLEM WE FACE ON OUR HIGH STREETS
🍺 Britain has lost nearly 1,800 pubs and bars since 2016, while the number of vape and tobacco shops has grown by 245 to almost 2,200 in the same period.
🏘️ Right now, anyone can open a vape shop without asking permission first, they get treated the same as a coffee shop or a clothes shop.
📉 This has let them pop up everywhere, especially in areas that are already struggling.
🎰 There are around 1,450 adult gaming centres across the UK, and more than half of these are in the poorest 20% of neighbourhoods.
📍 In the London Borough of Brent alone, there are more than 80 gambling venues.
WHAT WE'RE ANNOUNCING TODAY
🚀 Today marks a new step in putting power back in the hands of local communities.

🚭 The Prime Minister has announced that vape shops will need planning permission for the first time, stopping them opening near schools and closing the loophole that lets them pose as general convenience stores.
🎲 Adult Gaming Centres – the 24-hour fruit and slot machine lounges - will also need planning permission, closing another gap in the rules.

📋 The outdated "Aim to Permit" rule, which currently makes it hard for councils to say no to those gambling premises, will be scrapped. This will give councils a stronger say over whether new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops open in their area.

🎨 The government will also support councils to tidy up shopfronts and make high streets more welcoming, setting clearer standards for how high streets should look and sharing best practice from places already getting it right.📝 These changes will be consulted on shortly, followed by legislation as soon as we can.
AND WHY DOES THIS MATTER TO ME?
We want local people to feel the benefits of these changes in their everyday lives. These benefits include:
🗣️ A greater say over your high street

You'll finally have your concerns heard - councils will be able to refuse new gambling premises and vape shops where there are strong concerns from local residents, such as vape shops opening near schools, rather than being forced to approve them under outdated rules.
🛡️ Better-looking town centres

You'll start to see your local high street looking better, as government works with councils and the Planning Advisory Service over the next six months to show what good high street design looks like in practice - taking inspiration from high street success stories like Cross Street in Oswestry and Keynsham High Street.
🍻 A fairer deal for pubs and local venues

You'll benefit from a stronger local pub, social club and live music scene, with venues getting a 20% cut to their business rates from next year, partly paid for by reviewing tax breaks for businesses like vape shops that don't give much back to their local community.

title: Devolution explained: What new powers for local leaders means for you

content.content: WHAT IS DEVOLUTION?
🏛️ Devolution is the transfer of power away from Whitehall and into the hands of local leaders, such as mayors.
📍 Right now, the UK is overcentralised, with too many decisions made in Whitehall instead of in the towns and cities they affect.
📉 This has held back local economies and stopped places from reaching their full potential.
🤝 Devolution means decisions about your area get made by the people who understand their communities best.

🔑New powers being given to local leaders will give communities greater control over the decisions that shape jobs, transport, housing and public services in their area, as well as a share of income tax revenues for the first time.
DEVOLUTION IN ACTION

🚆 Devolution means five new train stations opening in the West Midlands, a key North East train line reopening to help local commuters get where they need to go, and buses being brought back under public control to be run for local people - not for profit.
🏗️ Devolution means regeneration that transforms town and city centres and restores a sense of pride, like the £100 million the West Midlands Mayor is investing in Coventry city centre.

🎓 Devolution means skills programmes tailored to local needs, such as in the North East, 65,000 residents have been supported to gain qualifications, opening up new employment opportunities in sectors including construction and childcare.
🤝 Devolution means empowering local leaders to deliver for their communities - from buses and housebuilding, to skills and opportunities. Devolution is at the heart of each one.
👥We currently have 14 mayors across England including in South Yorkshire, West of England and the East Midlands who are leading the front in terms of driving investment.
WHAT WE'RE ANNOUNCING TODAY
💰 Today marks the next crucial step in rewiring the country, putting power back in the hands of local people.
📣The Prime Minister has announced that Mayors will receive a share of income tax for the first time.
📈 And from next spring, mayors will also keep a greater share of locally generated revenues, starting with business rates.
🏙️ This means when places create jobs and grow their economies, they will now keep more of the rewards, giving local leaders new powers to invest in what matters most locally.
The Prime Minister has also announced further devolution of new powers including:
🚊Getting local transport schemes, trams and metros built faster by removing Whitehall barriers and speeding up approvals.
💡Backing local industries and innovative businesses, and attract investment, creating more well-paid jobs.
🏠 Building more homes where they're needed and unlocking stalled development sites.
AND WHY DOES THIS MATTER TO ME?
🚀 We've made huge steps forward in our devolution revolution, as we shift more power away from Westminster and into our communities.
🤝 We want to ensure local people continue to feel the benefits of devolution in their everyday lives. These benefits include:
🚌 Better transport

More control over rail and bus services means Mayors can crack on with the projects their areas need the most, helping communities stay connected. In the Liverpool City Region, Tap and Go has been rolled out on Merseyrail, with the rail service set to return to public control in 2028.
💼 More local opportunities

Mayors gaining more control over skills and employment support, including 16-19 funding, to help drive local job growth. This will let young people train for jobs employers need and give people out of work tailored support back into employment.
🏥 Better healthcare
In South Yorkshire and Greater Manchester, local leaders already have more control and accountability over how health services are run, so people get the healthcare they need, when they need it.
🏠 Unlocking new housing

Mayors using their powers to unlock more homes for their communities. In West Yorkshire, for example, a £334 million investment fund is helping to unlock land for development and back stalled sites, paving the way for thousands of new homes.

title: New GOV.UK page to stay updated on the octopus bloom
authors: Fisheries Management Team, Marine Management Organisation

content.content: Why MMO has launched this webpage

Since 2025, increasing numbers of common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) have been recorded in South West England. This increase, often known as an "octopus bloom", has generated a lot of interest across the fishing industry, government and the scientific community.
To help keep everyone informed, we, at the Marine Management Organisation (MMO), have launched a new webpage dedicated to the octopus bloom on GOV.UK.
A single place for the latest information
The new webpage brings together the latest information about the octopus bloom in English waters, making it easier to find updates in one place.
You’ll be able to access:
The octopus and shellfish infographics, previously shared through the South West Regional Fisheries Group will now be published on this webpage and continue to be updated every month.
🔗 MMO updates on the octopus bloom page on GOV.UK.
Help us build a clearer picture
We've also launched a new octopus reporting portal on this webpage.
Whether you’re a diver, recreational angler or member of the public, you can use the portal to report octopus sightings.
Every sighting helps. Combined with commercial fisheries data, these reports will help us better understand of where octopus are being found and whether they are appearing in new areas.
Supporting fisheries management plans

Both common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) and curled octopus (Eledone cirrhosa) are included in the Southern North Sea non-quota species fisheries management plan (FMP) and the Channel demersal non-quota species FMP.

Although these FMPs were developed before the increase in octopus sightings and landings seen in 2025, they already included actions to improve our understanding of octopus species through monitoring, research and evidence gathering.
Much of the work underway in response to the octopus bloom supports these FMP actions and will help us understand whether any additional steps may be needed in the future.
Working with the industry
We’re continuing to work closely with fishermen, scientists and other stakeholders while monitoring landings and gathering evidence.
This will help us better understand:
If you'd like to find out more, see the latest landings updates or report an octopus sighting, please visit the new webpage.
If you have any questions, contact us at FMP@marinemanagement.org.uk

description: Find the latest octopus landing data, research updates, and instructions for reporting sightings on the new octopus webpage from MMO.

title: How we’re making workplace technology more sustainable

content.content: When we think about sustainable technology, we don’t just think about the devices sat on our desks in front of us. We think about the whole journey: the materials used to make it, the energy it uses, how long it stays in service and what happens when it is no longer needed.

That is why sustainability is such an important part of our End User IT Services approach. We are still early in the work, so this is not a final results story. It is however a chance to share what we have started, what we are learning, and where colleagues across Defra group can help.
Why this matters to us

Our Digital Sustainability Strategy, published in October last year, sets out how we will make smarter and more responsible decisions about the technology we buy, use, reuse and recycle. For us, that means reducing the environmental impact of our devices, keeping them in use for longer and making sustainability part of everyday work.

One of the biggest changes is our move towards a more circular approach. Instead of treating laptops, phones and tablets as single-use products, we are looking at the whole life of each device. That starts with procuring remanufactured devices instead of buying brand new ones.

Remanufactured devices are used devices that are restored to meet the same quality standards as new devices. The devices are thoroughly inspected, repaired and rebuilt back to the manufacturer’s specification using a combination of both old and new parts where required. Keeping devices in service through maintenance, repair, reuse and recycling helps us reduce waste, lower emissions and make better use of finite resources.

In the first seven months of the contract we initiated with Atos last autumn, we have rolled out 6,012 remanufactured devices. That includes 4,190 laptops, 10 desktops, 345 tablets and 1,467 smartphones. This has resulted in an estimated saving of 1,400 tonnes of CO₂e emissions across the Defra IT estate. That is equivalent to taking around 320 passenger cars off the road for a year, or the annual energy use of around 500 homes.
Closing the loop on electronic waste
We have also taken an important step through our work with Closing the Loop, an organisation focused on electronic waste compensation and responsible recycling.

Two certificates were recently presented to Atos and Defra, recognising a “one-for-one” service across part of our mobile estate. In simple terms, for every new device introduced, an equivalent amount of electronic waste is collected and recycled responsibly. The certificates covered 1,468 mobile phones and 395 tablets.
How we’re enabling colleagues to get involved
The next stage is where this work becomes more visible to colleagues. We plan to run the first of our device amnesty initiatives during later this year.

These events will give colleagues a simple way to return old or unused devices so they can be reused, recycled or donated responsibly. They will also make it easier for everyone to play a part in reducing electronic waste.
This is the point where sustainability becomes practical and visible. It is also where small actions from many people can add up to something much bigger.
What colleagues can do now
Our chances of success depend on the choices we all make about the devices we use every day.

Using a remanufactured device, returning equipment we no longer need, or looking after the kit we have can all make a difference. While each action may seem small, together they reduce waste, keep valuable resources in use for longer, support the circular economy, and ensure better value for public money.

Which is why we are asking everyone to check whether they have any Defra devices they no longer use. Many people we recently contacted about having multiple devices told us they had an old one “in a drawer”. In the last six months, almost 10,000 devices have been returned, either through a device replacement project, or by staff taking action.
What we are working on next
We are also developing new services to help colleagues use devices more sustainably. These include:
Though these services are still being shaped, they will be an important part of the bigger picture, as this work develops.
Making digital sustainability part of everyday work

Our aim is to make sustainability part of everyday working, not something separate or additional. We are at the beginning of this journey, but the direction is clear. We want to make it easier to use technology for longer, and make sustainable choices part of normal service delivery.
There is more work in the pipeline, and we will continue to share updates as it develops.

This work is about more than improving our own services. It is helping to shape the future of sustainable technology across government. The sustainability commitments in the End User Services contract include remanufactured devices, electronic waste compensation, device amnesties and new sustainability-focused digital services.
For us, that is the most exciting part of this work. It shows how sustainability can be built into each stage of the technology lifecycle, and how public sector organisations can lead by example.
More information
Anna Fountain and Katie Bishop work in Defra’s digital sustainability team.
If you're interested in finding out more about what we do check out our LinkedIn page for all the latest news, stories and job openings. While you're there, why not give us a follow?
Like what you read? Subscribe to the blog for all the latest updates.

description: In Defra we are changing how we buy, use, reuse and recycle workplace technology. Anna Fountain and Katie Bishop update on how we are making this technology more sustainable, what we have learned so far, and their ideas for how we can enable Defra colleagues to get involved in supporting our digital sustainability aims.

title: Fighting Fire with Nature: How Healthy Landscapes Reduce Wildfire Risk

content.content: By Ruth Waters, Regional Director for the North of England, Operations Directorate, Natural England

The UK is facing a growing wildfire crisis this year, with prolonged hot, dry weather fuelling blazes across our moors, farmland and urban parks. This blog explores why wildfires are becoming more frequent and severe, the role climate change plays in heightening the risk, and the wider consequences for our landscapes and water supplies. It also sets out what Natural England is doing to reduce wildfire risk on its nature reserves, and how partnerships are helping to tackle the issue on the ground.

This year we are experiencing large scale wildfires devastating the UK’s landscapes, from our moors and dales to farmland and urban parks. Prolonged hot and dry weather has provided the ideal conditions for fires to take hold, which we have also seen in mainland Europe. France has declared their ongoing wildfire situation as the worst crisis to face the country since the Second World War.
What are wildfires and why have there been so many recently?

In the UK the term “wildfire” means any uncontrolled blaze on vegetation that needs action to extinguish. Virtually all wildfires in this country are caused by human activity, from the careless (e.g. negligent use of barbecues) to the deliberate (e.g. arson), as well as the inadvertent, such as agricultural equipment faults and “managed fires” (e.g. heather/grass burning) escaping control.

Our own records show that there have been over 240 reported wildfires this year on our most precious sites –Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) – including a 1,500 hectares fire in the Peak District (including Dove Stone RSPB reserve) which has damaged moorland valued for its blanket bog and heathland habitats, as well as breeding populations of birds such as golden plover and merlin. This fire was started by people setting off fireworks – so far one person from Greater Manchester has been charged with multiple criminal offences relating to the incident.

Most recently a fire at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk engulfed some 150 hectares, with the National Trust estimating it could take 25 years for the site to recover. At the height of the fire over 100 firefighters were needed to bring it under control, with hundreds of homes and caravans evacuated.
The consequences of climate change

Climate change is heightening the risk of wildfires. Extreme weather events are increasing, and like 2025, this summer has seen prolonged periods of dry weather alongside a series of record-breaking heatwaves across the world.

On 29th July, the Environment Agency announced that more than half of England was in drought. Looking more widely, Europe has warmed almost twice as fast as the global average. A warming atmosphere combined with prolonged dry conditions accelerates moisture removal from vegetation and soils. This creates an abundance of dry fuel for blazes to take hold and spread.

It’s not just the direct destruction from the fires themselves that we need to deal with. The bare, dry soil they leave behind repels water from the next rainfall event, causing run-off that can lead to soil erosion and flooding. In addition, sediment flowing into watercourses adds to the treatment costs for drinking water (over 70% of our drinking water comes from our uplands), which is then passed onto customers through higher water bills.
What is Natural England doing right now?

As a landowner ourselves, we continue to put measures in place on our National Nature Reserves (NNRs) to adapt and respond to increasing wildfire risk.  We are responsible for the management of over 130 NNRs – not all are at high risk from wildfire, but many are and climate change will see more of our NNRs at risk of either accidental or deliberate fires. We have developed wildfire emergency plans for our high-risk reserves that have information that will help our staff and the fire service in the event of fire such as access points, key-holders and muster points.

We ensure staff on high-risk sites have received specialist vegetation fire training provided through LANTRA and the Forestry Commission, and that we have the specialist equipment available to support fire and rescue services and to fight minor fires ourselves.

We incorporate fire reduction measures into our core site management. This reduces the ‘fuel’ available to a fire. For example, using firebreaks of broadleaved woodland and vegetation management such as grazing and cutting to stop a fire from spreading.

We use more active restoration measures to give nature a helping hand, like stone dams or bunds to hold back water in our peatlands, keeping water in the landscape for longer. Maintaining fire breaks and access routes also helps move firefighting equipment to isolated parts of our estate.

On our most vulnerable sites during periods of high fire risk, we present a more active, visible warden presence, supported by signage and publicity. This isn’t just aimed at deterring those who start fires deliberately, but at reducing the risk from accidental fires caused by discarded cigarettes or glass bottles or people using disposable barbeques.

Experience has demonstrated that where we are able to provide a high-profile warden presence that engages with the public constructively, fire incidents are reduced. In extreme cases we can temporally reduce access to an area to protect the public.

We work with partners across England on a number of wildfire issues.Nationally Natural England administers the Nature for Climate Peatland Grant Scheme, working with landowners and over 100 partners to rewet and restore peatlands, which hold more water in the landscape making it more difficult for fire to spread. Natural England are also part of the England and Wales Wildfire Forum which works to expand understanding of wildfires to reduce the impact they have.

At a local level, Natural England is a member of the Dorset Heaths Partnership which has been exploring ways to tackle wildfire issues since 2007. The Partnership includes site managers, the Fire and Rescue Service and the police.

The partners operate a WhatsApp group to both rapidly notify managers of a wildfire incident but also to coordinate water bowsers, equipment to cut and extend firebreaks and to advise the emergency services of site hazards and sensitive areas.

A dedicated partnership warden team works with local people, especially dog walkers, to rapidly report incidents and help engage with those that are unaware of the dangers of wildfire. Fire access points are all mapped and coded for ease of incident reporting and, more recently, QR codes have been added so the emergency services can get to the right locations quickly.
What Next?

A key finding of the latest adaptation report from the Climate Change Committee (CCC) - A Well-Adapted UK, is that coordination is lacking in a range of areas to manage the increasing risks to society from climate change. The report recommends the UK Government facilitates coordinated assessment and management of cascading climate risks between sectors and joint planning of the responses to extreme events (including wildfires).

At Natural England we have established a new Wildfire Project Group to co-ordinate the organisation’s work on wildfires, which is multi-faceted given our statutory duties as well as our landowner role. This group will review our procedures and ensure we continue to use the best available evidence to inform our decision-making and advice to Government. It will also consider our current approaches to more short-term wildfire mitigation measures, against the backdrop of our overall aim of recovering our ecosystems to bring long-term resilience to the growing challenges of climate change.

Natural England is also working closely with Defra, the Forestry Commission and Environment Agency on a co-ordinated approach to wildfire planning and response, feeding up to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) as overall department lead for wildfire.
